# Introduction

The Reject Inference (RI) problem concerns the challenge of learning from
outcomes that are observed exclusively for accepted applicants, while the
outcomes of rejected applicants remain unknown. This selective observation
induces acceptance bias (sample selection bias) and motivates statistical
methods for its identification and correction. While RI has been widely
studied in applied domains such as credit scoring, medical diagnosis, and
underwriting, it is fundamentally a missing-not-at-random (MNAR) data problem.
Although empirical results in the literature remain mixed—leading researchers
such as @HandHanley1993CanRIWork to question whether RI can be reliably
solved—its potential value in high-stakes decision systems continues to fuel
methodological development.

This work steps back from overly complex heuristics to examine RI from a
dynamic, feedback-driven perspective. Acceptance bias arises because past
selection decisions generate the biased historical data used to train future
models. These new models then make subsequent acceptance decisions, creating a
self-reinforcing feedback loop. Consequently, RI is inherently a dynamic
process. While several studies (e.g., @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL) utilize such
acceptance loops to generate synthetic data, prior work has not attempted to
exploit the dynamic structure of the loop itself. The underlying intuition is
clear: as a biased selection rule is repeatedly applied, the resulting bias
must either compound over time or stabilize within a sub-optimal equilibrium.

To investigate this hypothesis, this thesis establishes a formal and transparent
methodology. First, a review of existing literature highlights the key
criticisms and methodological gaps in RI that a dynamic perspective can address.
Second, responding to the critique by @ehrhardt2021rejectReview regarding the
lack of formal mathematical rigor in the field, I establish a precise
measure-theoretic formulation of the RI problem within credit scoring, isolating
inherent stochasticity from the institution's deterministic decision rules.
Third, I introduce a simulation framework based on a well-known two-class Linear
Discriminant Analysis (LDA) data-generating process. Fourth, I propose
*surprise* as a heuristic proxy to indirectly quantify acceptance bias. Fifth,
I evaluate whether surprise reliably approximates acceptance bias by examining
its relationship with logistic regression coefficient bias and cross-validation-based
cut-off selection. Finally, I discuss the implications of surprise-based metrics
for future RI methodologies.
